concepts.title: Books for Information versus Books That Speak
concepts.definition: John Ruskin separates all books into two classes: books of the moment -- temporary talk, print that informs for a day -- and books of all time, the good books whose voice rises from the grave of their authors to speak to every generation. The question 'what is a good book?' is answered by the test of permanence and voice.
concepts.key_idea: Books of the moment versus books of all time -- the good book is one whose voice outlives its author.
concepts.textbook_ref: keww135.txt opening sections (two classes of books, books of the moment, books of all time, voice from the grave of authors)
question_patterns: how does ruskin divide all books into two classes
in class 11 what is a good book: what are books of the moment
what does ruskin mean by the voice rising from the grave
why can newspapers not be called good books in ruskin's sense
what test decides whether a book belongs to all time
distinguish useful print from true literature according to ruskin

solution_steps.explain: Ruskin splits print into temporary, moment-serving matter and permanent, time-serving literature.
A good book speaks from the author's grave -- it was written to be true forever, not merely now.
Ask whether the book can still converse with readers centuries on; if yes, it is of all time.

concepts.title: The Authorship of the Good Book: Society's Best Work
concepts.definition: A good book, Ruskin argues, is the work not of one pen but of the best society of the author's age -- the accumulated insight, conscience and style of a nation distilled by one great mind. Words like 'canaille' and 'peerage' and 'national noblesse' mark his scale: a good book is aristocratic in the sense of being the best that a people could think and say.
concepts.key_idea: Written by one, authored by many -- the good book distils the best of a nation's mind into one voice.
concepts.textbook_ref: keww135.txt authorship sections (best society of the author's age, canaille, peerage, national noblesse, accumulated insight of a nation)
question_patterns: why does ruskin say a good book is written by a society not a man
in class 11 what is a good book: explain the terms canaille and national noblesse
how does the good book carry the best of its age
what is aristocratic about a good book in ruskin's special sense
relate the author's life to the book's lasting value
why does ruskin compare books with the peerage of a nation

solution_steps.explain: Behind the writer stands a century of accumulated thought -- the book is a nation's distillation.
Good books form a noblesse of intellect: chosen by merit of thought, not birth or rank.
Only the best a people thinks deserves the name -- hence the rarity and worth of true books.

concepts.title: Practical Advice: The Right Book, Read Right
concepts.definition: Ruskin ends in practical counsel: do not read too many books, but the right ones slowly; examine the border of each page, weigh the author's exact meaning, and refuse to be content with the canaille of current print. Reading a good book is an act of discipline and love, not a pastime to be consumed in heaps.
concepts.key_idea: Few books, read deep and slow -- Ruskin's reading discipline against the heap of momentary print.
concepts.textbook_ref: keww135.txt counsel sections (do not read too many, examine the border of the page, weigh the author's meaning, refuse the canaille of print, reading as discipline)
question_patterns: what advice does ruskin give about the number of books to read
in class 11 what is a good book: what does ruskin mean by examining the border of the page
why should readers refuse the canaille of current print
how does slow reading differ from devouring books
explain reading as an act of discipline in ruskin's terms
apply ruskin's advice to choosing books in the age of abundance

solution_steps.explain: Fewer books, better chosen -- reading heaps of momentary print wastes the attention that makes good books yield.
Study the exact wording -- the border of the page -- and weigh what the author precisely meant.
Treat good books as the noblest society available, and give them the love and discipline that company deserves.

worked_examples.question_pattern: A friend says a well-researched newspaper report is a good book by Ruskin's standard. Test the claim.

solution_template.explain: The report may be true, useful and even admirable for its day.
Ruskin's good book must speak to every generation; the report serves only its own.
It belongs to the books of the moment -- excellent talk, but not literature of all time.

worked_examples.question_pattern: A student reads forty novels a year but remembers none. What would Ruskin advise?

solution_template.explain: Heaping up momentary print with no examination is exactly the 'read too many' fault.
Choose fewer, better books; read slowly, weighing the exact meaning of the author.
Depth of company with one good book outweighs a warehouse of consumed ones.
